IDiscussionBoardAdminuser.description:
Detailed administrator user profile mapped to the `discussion_board_adminusers` Prisma model.

This DTO is returned by administrator-focused read and update operations such as GET or PUT `/discussionBoard/adminUser/adminUsers/{adminUserId}`. It represents the full business profile of an administrator account, exposing identification, contact, lifecycle status, and audit information that is safe to surface to other authorized admins.

Sensitive authentication internals such as the `password_hash` column or any token-related data are intentionally excluded even though they exist on the underlying table. The field set instead focuses on profile metadata and operational flags that are necessary for account management, moderation, and audit tooling.

id.description:
Unique identifier of the administrator user in the `discussion_board_adminusers` table.

This value corresponds directly to the `id` primary key column, which is stored as a UUID in the database. It is used as the path parameter value for administrator detail and update endpoints and forms the stable handle for all foreign-key and audit relationships referencing this admin account.

displayName.description:
Public or semi-public display name of the administrator account.

This property maps to the non-nullable `display_name` column on the `discussion_board_adminusers` Prisma model. It is shown in administrative user interfaces, moderation actions, and audit logs so that humans can easily recognize which administrator performed a given operation.

email.description:
Primary email address associated with this administrator account.

This property reflects the non-nullable, unique `email` column in the `discussion_board_adminusers` table. It is used for authentication flows, administrative notifications, and contact in case of security or policy issues. The value must be a well-formed email address and must remain unique among all administrator records.

bio.description:
Optional short profile or role description for this administrator account.

This property maps to the nullable `bio` column on the `discussion_board_adminusers` Prisma model. It can contain free-form text describing the administrator’s responsibilities, team, or role in the organization. When no description has been provided, the value is stored as null in the database and may be omitted from user interface displays.

emailVerified.description:
Indicates whether the administrator’s email address has been verified.

This flag is backed by the non-nullable `email_verified` boolean column on the `discussion_board_adminusers` table. A value of `true` means the admin has successfully passed the email verification process, while `false` usually restricts access to certain high-risk operations until verification is completed. Changes to this field should be driven by controlled verification workflows or privileged administrative tools.

accountStatus.description:
Lifecycle status of the administrator account controlling whether the admin can actively use the system.

This value corresponds to the non-nullable `account_status` column on the `discussion_board_adminusers` Prisma model. Typical business values include states such as `active`, `suspended`, or `closed`, and they determine whether the admin may authenticate and perform moderation tasks. The exact domain of allowed values is enforced by application-level business rules rather than this schema.

createdAt.description:
Timestamp indicating when this administrator account record was first created.

This property mirrors the non-nullable `created_at` `DateTime` column in the `discussion_board_adminusers` table. It is generated by the persistence layer at insert time and is used for audit trails, chronological sorting in management screens, and reporting on the growth of administrative staff over time.

updatedAt.description:
Timestamp of the most recent update to this administrator account record.

This property reflects the non-nullable `updated_at` `DateTime` column on the `discussion_board_adminusers` Prisma model. It is automatically updated whenever profile metadata or status flags on this admin account change, allowing tooling to determine how fresh the displayed information is and to support concurrency controls where needed.

deletedAt.description:
Soft deletion timestamp for this administrator account, if it has been logically removed.

This property maps to the nullable `deleted_at` column in the `discussion_board_adminusers` table. When the value is a date-time, the account is considered soft-deleted and should no longer be usable for authentication or regular operations, although it may still appear in audit views. When the value is null, the account is considered not soft-deleted.

lastLoginAt.description:
Timestamp of the last successful login for this administrator account.

This property corresponds to the nullable `last_login_at` `DateTime` column on the `discussion_board_adminusers` model. It is updated whenever the admin successfully authenticates and is primarily used for security reviews, detecting stale accounts, and providing visibility in account management dashboards about when an admin last accessed the system.

IDiscussionBoardAdminuser.IUpdate.description:
Update payload for a discussionBoard administrator user profile.

This DTO represents the subset of columns on the `discussion_board_adminusers` Prisma model that are allowed to change through profile maintenance APIs. It intentionally excludes identity and authentication-related fields such as the primary key and `password_hash`, focusing instead on profile metadata and account lifecycle flags.

All properties are optional so that clients can perform partial updates. The service layer is responsible for applying validation rules, enforcing uniqueness constraints on the `email` column, and controlling which actors are allowed to change sensitive flags such as `email_verified` or `account_status`.

email.description:
Administrator email address used for authentication and notifications.

This property maps directly to the non-nullable, unique `email` column of the `discussion_board_adminusers` table. During an update, the value may be changed to reflect a new contact address, but the service must ensure that the email remains unique among all administrator accounts and that it conforms to standard email formatting rules.

display_name.description:
Display name of the administrator account in snake_case form.

This field writes to the `display_name` column on the `discussion_board_adminusers` Prisma model. It is maintained for compatibility with code paths or generators that refer to the column name directly. Clients may supply either this snake_case property or the camelCase `displayName` property to update the administrator’s human-readable name.

displayName.description:
Human-readable display name of the administrator account in camelCase form.

This property is a convenience alias for the underlying `display_name` column in the `discussion_board_adminusers` table. It is typically preferred in TypeScript and JSON APIs where camelCase naming is standard, while still updating the same database column and carrying the same semantic meaning as the `display_name` property.

bio.description:
Optional short profile or role description for this administrator.

This property maps to the nullable `bio` column on the `discussion_board_adminusers` Prisma model. Providing a non-null value stores or updates the description, while explicitly sending null clears the existing text. The text may be surfaced in internal administrative interfaces to provide context about the admin’s responsibilities.

email_verified.description:
Email verification flag for the administrator account in snake_case form.

This property writes to the `email_verified` boolean column on the `discussion_board_adminusers` table. It is kept for compatibility with column-oriented naming. Only controlled workflows or privileged administrative tools should update this flag, as it indicates whether the admin’s email address has been successfully verified.

emailVerified.description:
Email verification flag for the administrator account in camelCase form.

This property is a camelCase alias for the `email_verified` column of the `discussion_board_adminusers` Prisma model. Setting this value to true or false updates the same underlying field as `email_verified` and should follow the same business rules and audit requirements related to email verification.

account_status.description:
Lifecycle status of the administrator account in snake_case form.

This property updates the `account_status` column on the `discussion_board_adminusers` table. It is maintained in snake_case for callers or tooling that work directly with database column names. Typical values include `active`, `suspended`, or `closed`, and they control whether the admin may authenticate and perform moderation duties.

accountStatus.description:
Lifecycle status of the administrator account in camelCase form.

This property is a camelCase alias for the `account_status` column in the `discussion_board_adminusers` model. It updates the same underlying field as `account_status` but aligns with usual JSON and TypeScript naming conventions. Application-level rules determine which status values are allowed and what effects they have on administrator capabilities.

IDiscussionBoardMemberuser.ISummary.description:
Summary view of a discussion board member user, optimized for list views, embeddings, and moderation tooling.

This DTO is backed by the `discussion_board_memberusers` Prisma model and exposes only public and moderation-relevant scalar fields, avoiding any sensitive authentication data or reverse collections.

It is typically embedded into other response DTOs (for example, report or comment views) whenever a compact representation of the member user is required without loading the full account record.

id.description:
Unique identifier of the member user in the discussion board system.

This value maps directly to `discussion_board_memberusers.id` and is used as the stable primary key for joins and references in other entities such as articles, comments, and reports.

display_name.description:
Public display name or nickname for the member user.

This property corresponds to the `discussion_board_memberusers.display_name` column and is shown alongside articles, comments, and other user-generated content.

It is intentionally included in the summary so that UIs can render meaningful author or reporter labels without fetching the full member user detail record.

account_status.description:
High-level lifecycle state of the member user account.

This field is mapped from the `discussion_board_memberusers.account_status` column and indicates whether the account is active, suspended, closed, banned, or in a similar business-defined state.

Including this value in the summary allows moderation and administrative views to quickly assess whether the reporter or author is currently restricted or fully active.

created_at.description:
Timestamp when this member user account was created.

This value is sourced from the `discussion_board_memberusers.created_at` column and is useful for sorting and for quickly understanding the relative age of an account in list and audit views.

IDiscussionBoardAdminuser.ISummary.description:
Summary view of a discussion board administrator user account derived from the discussion_board_adminusers Prisma model.

This DTO is optimized for administrative list screens, moderation history, and audit trails where many administrator rows are shown at once. It exposes only non-sensitive profile, contact, status, and activity fields that are safe to include in responses while still allowing operators to quickly identify who an admin is and what state their account is in.

The summary aligns closely with the underlying database columns: it includes identifiers, the administrator’s email and display name, key lifecycle flags such as email verification and account_status, and important timestamps like created_at and last_login_at. Sensitive authentication details such as password_hash are never exposed here, and fields that would require full-detail views can be added through more specific DTOs if needed.

id.description:
Unique identifier of the administrator account in the discussion board system.

This value corresponds directly to the `id` primary key column in the `discussion_board_adminusers` Prisma model and is generated as a UUID when the admin account is created.

It is used throughout the system as the stable reference for linking sessions, moderation actions, and audit records back to this admin user.

email.description:
Login and contact email address for the administrator account.

This value maps to the `email` column in the `discussion_board_adminusers` table, which is unique among administrator accounts. It is used both for authentication and for delivering critical notifications such as security alerts or moderation workflow messages.

In list and summary views, this field helps operations staff quickly identify the specific admin account they are inspecting or acting upon.

display_name.description:
Human-friendly display name for the administrator shown in dashboards, logs, and moderation views.

This property corresponds to the non-nullable `display_name` column in the `discussion_board_adminusers` Prisma model. It is the primary name shown to other administrators when attributing actions, such as “article removed by {display_name}”.

Unlike internal identifiers, the display name is intended to be easily recognizable and may follow organizational naming conventions or role-based labels.

profile_image_url.description:
Optional public URL of the administrator's profile image used in the UI.

This value is expected to be a pre-uploaded URL pointing to an image stored in an external storage service (for example, an object storage bucket or CDN). The backend never accepts raw binary or base64 image data in this field; only the resolved URL is persisted and exposed.

When not set or when the administrator has not configured an avatar, this property may be omitted from responses and client applications should fall back to a default placeholder image.

email_verified.description:
Flag indicating whether the administrator's email address has been verified.

This property reflects the `email_verified` column in the `discussion_board_adminusers` Prisma model. When true, the account has successfully completed whatever email verification process the system requires, which may be a prerequisite for performing sensitive actions.

In administrative summaries, this field helps security and platform teams quickly identify accounts that are operating with unverified contact details and may require additional review or restrictions.

account_status.description:
Lifecycle status code representing the current state of the administrator account.

This property corresponds to the non-nullable `account_status` column in the `discussion_board_adminusers` table. Typical business values include states such as `active`, `suspended`, or `closed`, but the exact set of codes is defined by the domain.

In list views, this field allows operators to see at a glance whether an admin can sign in and exercise privileges, or whether access has been restricted due to policy violations, security concerns, or organizational changes.

created_at.description:
Timestamp indicating when the administrator account record was created.

The value maps to the `created_at` column in the `discussion_board_adminusers` Prisma model and is stored as an ISO 8601 date-time in UTC. It typically corresponds to the moment the account was first registered or provisioned by another admin.

This field is frequently used in audit and reporting contexts to understand how long an administrator has existed in the system and to segment accounts by tenure or onboarding wave.

last_login_at.description:
Timestamp of the most recent successful login for this administrator account, when available.

This property reflects the nullable `last_login_at` column in the `discussion_board_adminusers` table. When present, it indicates the last time the admin successfully authenticated and began a session. For newly created or unused accounts, this column may be null and the field may be omitted in responses.

Administrative dashboards can use this value to highlight dormant accounts, detect unusual activity patterns, or support security reviews by showing when an admin last accessed the system.

scenario.draft:
Validate that a first-time guest visitor can successfully join the discussion board as an anonymous placeholder account.

Workflow:
1. Client generates a fresh opaque anonymous_token that has never been used before and calls POST /auth/guestUser/join with a well-formed IDiscussionBoardGuestUser.IJoin payload including anonymous_token, and realistic href/referrer/ip context.
2. Server checks discussion_board_guestusers for an existing row with this anonymous_token and finds none, so it inserts a new record with a new uuid id, anonymous_token, created_at, updated_at, and null deleted_at.
3. Server issues a new guestUser JWT token pair (access/refresh) wrapped in IAuthorizationToken and returns an IDiscussionBoardGuestUser.IAuthorized response containing the new id, the same anonymous_token, timestamps, and token metadata.
4. Test asserts HTTP 201/200 success status, validates that the response anonymous_token exactly matches the request token, that deleted_at is null, created_at and updated_at are present and in ISO date-time format, and that token.access/refresh/expired_at/refreshable_until are all non-empty and consistent.
5. Optionally perform a quick authenticated call using the returned access token to ensure the token is actually usable in the rest of the API surface (if such endpoints are available in the broader test suite).

dependencies.purpose:
Essential authentication prerequisite:
This join operation (post /auth/guestUser/join) must be executed before any operations requiring 'guestUser' actor authorization.
It establishes the necessary user account and authentication context for the 'guestUser' actor, enabling subsequent API calls that depend on this specific authorization level.
Without this join operation, the main scenario endpoint and its dependencies will fail due to insufficient authentication credentials.

scenario.draft:
Verify that when a guest with an existing active placeholder account (same anonymous_token, deleted_at null) calls join again, the system reuses the existing guest record rather than creating a duplicate, while still issuing fresh tokens.

Workflow:
1. First call POST /auth/guestUser/join with a given anonymous_token value T1 to materialize an initial guest record and capture the returned IDiscussionBoardGuestUser.IAuthorized, including id and timestamps.
2. Call POST /auth/guestUser/join again with the exact same anonymous_token T1, possibly with updated href/referrer/ip context.
3. Server looks up discussion_board_guestusers by anonymous_token T1, finds the existing record with deleted_at null, and chooses to reuse it according to business rules, updating updated_at but not created_at.
4. Server issues a new pair of JWT tokens and returns an IDiscussionBoardGuestUser.IAuthorized response.
5. Test asserts that the id in the second response matches the id from the first join, that anonymous_token is identical, created_at is unchanged, updated_at is greater than or equal to the previous updated_at, and deleted_at remains null.
6. Test also verifies that the second response contains a different access token string from the first response, confirming that new credentials are produced while the account identity is stable.

scenario.draft:
Validate how guest join behaves when the underlying guest record was previously marked as deleted (deleted_at not null) but the same anonymous_token is presented again, ensuring that the system follows the defined business rule (e.g., restore vs. reject).

Workflow:
1. Using lower-layer tools or administrative operations available in the test environment, ensure a discussion_board_guestusers row exists with a chosen anonymous_token T2, a valid id, created_at and updated_at timestamps, and a non-null deleted_at value that marks the guest as closed. (If an admin API exists elsewhere in the system to soft-delete or close guests, the test should use it; otherwise, this precondition is arranged by fixtures.)
2. Call POST /auth/guestUser/join with anonymous_token T2 and reasonable href/referrer/ip context.
3. Depending on the defined business rule, the system should either:
   a) Restore the existing record by clearing deleted_at and updating updated_at, then issue new tokens; or
   b) Reject the join indicating that the guest identity is closed and may not be reused.
4. For case (a) restore: assert a 200/201 success; verify that the returned id matches the preexisting record id, deleted_at is now null, updated_at is more recent, and a valid token bundle is returned.
5. For case (b) reject: assert an appropriate 4xx error code, with an error body that clearly signals that the guest is closed and cannot be rejoined; ensure that no new guest record is created and the existing one is unchanged.
6. Also verify that the response never leaks internal details like hashed tokens or underlying storage fields not described in IDiscussionBoardGuestUser.IAuthorized.

scenario.draft:
Ensure that an active guest user with a valid refresh token can obtain a fresh set of JWT tokens via the refresh endpoint.

Workflow:
1. Call POST /auth/guestUser/join with a new anonymous_token to create an active guest placeholder record and capture the IDiscussionBoardGuestUser.IAuthorized response, including the token.refresh value.
2. Construct an IDiscussionBoardGuestUser.IRefresh payload using the captured refreshToken and realistic href/referrer/ip context, then call POST /auth/guestUser/refresh.
3. Server validates the refresh token (integrity, expiration, and association with an existing discussion_board_guestusers.id whose deleted_at is null) and, on success, issues a new access token and potentially a new refresh token.
4. Test asserts HTTP 200 success, confirms that the response contains a valid IDiscussionBoardGuestUser.IAuthorized structure, and verifies that:
   - The id and anonymous_token in the refresh response match those returned from the original join.
   - The new access token string differs from the original one, proving rotation.
   - Depending on implementation, the refresh token may change or remain the same; the test should capture and assert whichever behavior is documented but must at least verify that token.refresh is present and non-empty.
   - updated_at is greater than or equal to the value from the join response, reflecting recent activity.
5. Optionally, perform a quick authenticated call on some guest-allowed endpoint using the new access token to ensure it is usable.

scenario.draft:
Verify that the refresh endpoint rejects refresh attempts that use an expired, malformed, or tampered refresh token, without issuing new credentials or leaking sensitive details.

Workflow:
1. Call POST /auth/guestUser/join with a new anonymous_token to obtain an initial authorized session and a valid refresh token.
2. Derive several invalid refresh token cases, such as:
   - A token with an altered character in the middle (simulated tampering).
   - A token with a completely different structure (e.g., random string) that fails signature/format checks.
   - If the test environment supports time manipulation or preconfigured expired tokens, a token that is structurally valid but past its expiration.
3. For each invalid token, construct an IDiscussionBoardGuestUser.IRefresh payload and call POST /auth/guestUser/refresh.
4. Assert that each call returns an appropriate 4xx client error (e.g., 400 or 401), that the response does not include any IAuthorizationToken fields, and that no new guest record is created or modified.
5. If error codes or messages are standardized, verify that the error body clearly indicates invalid or expired refresh token without revealing cryptographic or internal token details.

Confirm that when the guest placeholder account backing a refresh token has been logically deleted (deleted_at set), the refresh operation is refused and no new tokens are issued.

Workflow:
1. Call POST /auth/guestUser/join with a new anonymous_token to create an active guest record and capture the IDiscussionBoardGuestUser.IAuthorized response, including id and token.refresh.

4. Server validates the token, resolves the associated guest id, detects that deleted_at is non-null, and rejects the refresh request without issuing new tokens.
5. Test asserts an appropriate 4xx response (such as 403 or 410) and verifies that the body does not contain a token field or any IAuthorizationToken structure.
6. If error semantics are defined (e.g., specific error code for deactivated identity), assert that the response matches those semantics, ensuring clear communication that the identity is closed rather than the token being merely malformed.

scenario.draft: Test successful registration of a new discussion board member user. Steps: (1) Call POST /auth/memberUser/join with a unique, valid email, strong password, and valid displayName plus realistic href/referrer and optional profile fields. (2) Assert response status is 201 or 200 as specified, and body matches IDiscussionBoardMemberuser.IAuthorized shape. (3) Verify returned token.access and token.refresh are non-empty strings and expired_at/refreshable_until are valid future ISO timestamps. (4) Verify core identity fields (id as UUID, email equals request email, display_name equals request displayName, email_verified and account_status follow initial business rules). (5) Optionally, in DB or via subsequent authenticated calls (if available), ensure that a discussion_board_memberusers record was created with correct values and that lifecycle fields like created_at and updated_at are set.

Test that member registration enforces email uniqueness at the business level. Steps: (1) Call POST /auth/memberUser/join with a specific email and valid password/displayName to create an account. (2) Immediately call POST /auth/memberUser/join again with the same email but possibly different password/displayName. (3) Expect the second call to fail with a 4xx client error indicating duplicate or already-registered email. (4) Verify that no additional member user record is created for the same email and that only one active account exists for that email. (5) Confirm that no new token pair is issued for the rejected registration attempt.

Test handling of optional profile fields during member registration. scenario.draft:

import { ArrayUtil, RandomGenerator, TestValidator } from "@nestia/e2e";
import { IConnection } from "@nestia/fetcher";
import typia, { tags } from "typia";

import api from "@ORGANIZATION/PROJECT-api";
import type { IAuthorizationToken } from "@ORGANIZATION/PROJECT-api/lib/structures/IAuthorizationToken";
import type { IDiscussionBoardAdminUserJoin } from "@ORGANIZATION/PROJECT-api/lib/structures/IDiscussionBoardAdminUserJoin";
import type { IDiscussionBoardAdminuser } from "@ORGANIZATION/PROJECT-api/lib/structures/IDiscussionBoardAdminuser";

/**
 * Verify idempotent-like delete semantics for missing member user restriction.
 *
 * Business goal: When an admin user attempts to delete (lift) a restriction for
 * a member user that does not currently have a restriction row in
 * `discussion_board_memberuser_restrictions`, the backend must respond with an
 * error instead of succeeding silently, and it must not create or modify any
 * restriction records as a side effect.
 *
 * Available APIs:
 *
 * - POST /auth/adminUser/join -> api.functional.auth.adminUser.join -> body:
 *   IDiscussionBoardAdminUserJoin.IRequest -> response:
 *   IDiscussionBoardAdminuser.IAuthorized (sets Authorization header)
 * - DELETE /discussionBoard/adminUser/memberUsers/{memberUserId}/restriction ->
 *   api.functional.discussionBoard.adminUser.memberUsers.restriction.erase ->
 *   props: { memberUserId: string & tags.Format<"uuid"> } -> response: void |
 *   HttpError
 *
 * Constraints and limitations:
 *
 * - We do not have any API to create or read member users or their restrictions,
 *   so we cannot deterministically ensure the chosen memberUserId belongs to an
 *   existing or non-existing restriction record. Instead, we rely on a freshly
 *   generated random UUID as a highly likely non-existent memberUserId, which
 *   is acceptable for this test harness.
 * - We cannot verify via GET that no restriction row was created as a side effect
 *   of the failed DELETE because no such read/search API is available in the
 *   provided SDK. Therefore, we restrict our validation to ensuring that
 *   attempting to erase a restriction for this memberUserId results in an
 *   error, not a successful void response.
 * - We must not manipulate `connection.headers` directly in the test. All
 *   authentication header handling is done internally by the SDK implementation
 *   of `auth.adminUser.join`.
 * - We must not assert on specific HTTP status codes; instead, we only assert
 *   that some error is thrown. Status-specific testing using TestValidator
 *   helpers like httpError or manual HttpError inspection is prohibited.
 *
 * Test steps:
 *
 * 1. Register and authenticate a discussion board admin user using
 *    `api.functional.auth.adminUser.join`, providing a valid
 *    IDiscussionBoardAdminUserJoin.IRequest body.
 *
 *    - Use typia.random to generate structurally valid values, but we can override
 *         email/href/referrer with RandomGenerator / manual strings where
 *         convenient as long as they satisfy the Format tags.
 *    - After this call, the SDK will automatically store the access token in
 *         `connection.headers.Authorization`, so subsequent calls are
 *         authorized as this admin user.
 * 2. Generate a random memberUserId using `typia.random<string &
 *    tags.Format<"uuid">>()`. This UUID is extremely unlikely to match any
 *    existing member user restriction record, approximating the "no
 *    restriction" case required by the scenario.
 * 3. Call `api.functional.discussionBoard.adminUser.memberUsers.restriction.erase`
 *    with the authenticated connection and the random memberUserId.
 * 4. Use `await TestValidator.error("delete restriction on missing record must
 *    fail", async () => { ... })` to assert that the erase call throws an error
 *    (most likely an HttpError signaling not-found or similar). We do not
 *    attempt to inspect the error type or status code, only that an error
 *    occurs.
 * 5. Because we have no read or listing API for restrictions, we cannot validate
 *    that no record was created as a side effect. However, by design erase
 *    performs a hard delete, and in the missing-row case it should not succeed.
 *    Therefore, verifying that an error occurs for a random memberUserId is
 *    sufficient to confirm that the backend does not treat a missing record as
 *    a silent success.
 */
export async function test_api_admin_member_user_restriction_delete_idempotency_for_missing_record(
  connection: api.IConnection,
) {
  // 1. Register and authenticate an admin user
  const joinBody = {
    email: typia.random<string & tags.Format<"email">>(),
    password: typia.random<string & tags.Format<"password">>(),
    display_name: RandomGenerator.name(),
    bio: RandomGenerator.paragraph(),
    ip: null,
    href: typia.random<string & tags.Format<"uri">>(),
    referrer: typia.random<string & tags.Format<"uri">>(),
  } satisfies IDiscussionBoardAdminUserJoin.IRequest;

  const admin: IDiscussionBoardAdminuser.IAuthorized =
    await api.functional.auth.adminUser.join(connection, {
      body: joinBody,
    });
  typia.assert(admin);

  // 2. Prepare a random memberUserId that almost certainly has no restriction
  const memberUserId: string & tags.Format<"uuid"> = typia.random<
    string & tags.Format<"uuid">
  >();

  // 3-4. Attempt to delete restriction for the non-existent member user
  await TestValidator.error(
    "delete restriction on missing member user must fail",
    async () => {
      await api.functional.discussionBoard.adminUser.memberUsers.restriction.erase(
        connection,
        {
          memberUserId,
        },
      );
    },
  );
}

scenario.draft:
Test the complete lifecycle of a member user restriction managed by an admin: create, update, and delete.

Workflow:
1. Call POST /auth/adminUser/join to create and authenticate an adminUser.
2. With the adminUser token, call POST /discussionBoard/adminUser/memberUsers/{memberUserId}/restriction to create an initial restriction with specific values for restriction_level, reason_category, started_at, and optionally ended_at.
3. Call PUT /discussionBoard/adminUser/memberUsers/{memberUserId}/restriction to adjust the restriction, such as changing restriction_level and setting an ended_at that defines when the restriction should end.
4. Validate that the PUT response returns the updated IDiscussionBoardMemberuserRestriction entity reflecting the new values and an updated updated_at timestamp.
5. Finally, call DELETE /discussionBoard/adminUser/memberUsers/{memberUserId}/restriction to lift the restriction.
6. Assert that the DELETE response is successful and that subsequent reads of restriction state (via an existing GET restriction API) show that there is no active restriction for the member user, confirming the full lifecycle works as expected and that each operation respects the one-row-per-member invariant.

scenario.draft:
Verify that an authenticated admin user can successfully update all available notification preference flags (activity, digest, marketing) in a single call and that the changes persist.

Scenario steps:
1. Call POST /auth/adminUser/join to register a new admin user and obtain JWT access token for the adminUser actor.
2. Optionally call GET /discussionBoard/adminUser/notifications/adminUser/preferences (already covered elsewhere) to observe initial default values; this step is implicit in this scenario and not required for setup.
3. Call PUT /discussionBoard/adminUser/notifications/adminUser/preferences with a body that sets:
   - activity_notifications_enabled = true
   - digest_notifications_enabled = true
   - marketing_notifications_enabled = false
4. Assert that the response status indicates success and that the response body IDiscussionBoardAdminuserNotificationPreference reflects the new boolean values.
5. Optionally re-call GET /discussionBoard/adminUser/notifications/adminUser/preferences to ensure values are persisted.

Business validations:
- Only the authenticated admin’s own preferences are updated; there is no way to change another admin’s row.
- All three flags are handled atomically: the record reflects the combination sent in the request, not a partial update.
- System-managed fields created_at remains unchanged and updated_at is advanced.

dependencies.purpose: Create a new adminUser account and obtain JWT tokens so that we have an authenticated admin context for updating notification preferences.

scenario.draft:
Verify that the admin notification preference update endpoint correctly performs partial updates when only a subset of flags is supplied, leaving unspecified flags unchanged.

Scenario steps:
1. Call POST /auth/adminUser/join to register a new admin user and obtain JWT access token.
2. Call PUT /discussionBoard/adminUser/notifications/adminUser/preferences with an initial body setting all flags explicitly (e.g., activity_notifications_enabled = true, digest_notifications_enabled = false, marketing_notifications_enabled = false) to establish a known baseline.
3. Call PUT /discussionBoard/adminUser/notifications/adminUser/preferences again, this time including only activity_notifications_enabled = false in the body and omitting the other fields.
4. Assert that the response shows:
   - activity_notifications_enabled changed from true to false.
   - digest_notifications_enabled and marketing_notifications_enabled remain at their previous baseline values.
5. Optionally re-fetch preferences via GET /discussionBoard/adminUser/notifications/adminUser/preferences to confirm persistence of the partial update behavior.

Business validations:
- The service treats missing fields as "no change" rather than resetting them to defaults.
- updated_at reflects the time of the second update, while created_at remains the original creation time.
- Only the authenticated admin’s own row is impacted by these calls.

dependencies.purpose: Create an adminUser account and obtain authorization context for subsequent preference updates.

scenario.draft:
Validate that an admin user can repeatedly opt in and out of marketing notifications and that the marketing_notifications_enabled flag flips accordingly across multiple updates without affecting other flags.

Scenario steps:
1. Call POST /auth/adminUser/join to register a new admin user and get an access token.
2. Call PUT /discussionBoard/adminUser/notifications/adminUser/preferences with body setting marketing_notifications_enabled = true and reasonable defaults for the other flags (e.g., activity_notifications_enabled = true, digest_notifications_enabled = false).
3. Assert that the response shows marketing_notifications_enabled = true.
4. Call PUT /discussionBoard/adminUser/notifications/adminUser/preferences again with body setting marketing_notifications_enabled = false only.
5. Assert that the response now shows marketing_notifications_enabled = false while activity_notifications_enabled and digest_notifications_enabled retain their previous values.
6. Optionally repeat the toggle once more to confirm idempotent flipping behavior.

Business validations:
- The admin can freely change their marketing opt-in status, and each request accurately reflects the latest preference.
- The endpoint does not impose one-way restrictions (no forced opt-in).
- Other flags are not unintentionally modified when only marketing_notifications_enabled is provided.

scenario.draft:
Ensure that updating admin notification preferences is forbidden without a valid adminUser authentication context and cannot be accessed by unauthenticated callers.

Scenario steps:
1. Without calling any auth endpoints, attempt to call PUT /discussionBoard/adminUser/notifications/adminUser/preferences with a valid-looking body.
2. Assert that the response returns an authorization error (such as 401 Unauthorized or 403 Forbidden) and does not expose preference data.
3. Optionally, repeat with an invalid or expired token if the test framework supports constructing such tokens, still expecting an authorization failure.

Business validations:
- The endpoint strictly requires an authenticated adminUser; anonymous callers cannot read or modify preferences.
- No preference record is created or modified when the call is unauthorized.
- Error responses do not leak sensitive internal details about admin accounts or preference storage.

scenario.draft:
Verify that the admin notification preference update endpoint ignores any attempt by a client to spoof the target admin identity and always uses the authenticated adminUser from the token.

Scenario steps:
1. Call POST /auth/adminUser/join to register an admin user (Admin A) and obtain JWT access token.
2. Using Admin A’s token, call PUT /discussionBoard/adminUser/notifications/adminUser/preferences with a body that includes only valid preference fields. (Even if the DTO does not define identity fields, this step confirms normal behavior for Admin A.)
3. If the implementation allows sending extraneous fields in the JSON payload, craft a second PUT call where the client attempts to include an identity-like field (e.g., a non-schema property) pointing to a different admin’s hypothetical id. Even though this field is non-schema and ignored, the test narrative focuses on verifying that the resulting stored preferences still belong to Admin A.
4. After the second update, call GET /discussionBoard/adminUser/notifications/adminUser/preferences (covered elsewhere) using Admin A’s token and assert that the preferences reflect only Admin A’s changes and that no cross-account modification is possible.

Business validations:
- The endpoint determines the target row purely from the authenticated admin context and not from any client-supplied identifiers.
- Attempts to spoof identity in the request body do not cause updates to any other admin’s notification preferences.
- The behavior is stable across multiple requests from the same admin account.

scenario.draft:
Confirm that admin notification preference updates are independent of article, category, like, comment, attachment, restriction, and report data, i.e., they can succeed in a clean system with no content created.

Scenario steps:
1. Call POST /auth/adminUser/join to create a new admin user and obtain JWT tokens.

3. Assert that the response indicates success and that the returned IDiscussionBoardAdminuserNotificationPreference reflects the requested values.
4. Optionally verify that repeated calls with different combinations still succeed without any content-dependent prerequisites.

Business validations:
- The endpoint has no hidden dependencies on discussion_board_articles, discussion_board_article_categories, discussion_board_article_likes, discussion_board_comments, discussion_board_attachments, discussion_board_memberuser_restrictions, or discussion_board_reports.
- Admins can configure their notification preferences even before any content or reports exist in the system.
- The behavior remains consistent regardless of the presence or absence of related content records.

scenario.draft:
Test successful JWT token refresh for a member user.

Workflow:
1. Prepare an existing authenticated member user context using a prior join or login flow (assumed to have already issued a valid refresh token conforming to IDiscussionBoardMemberUserRefresh.IRequest).
2. Client calls POST /auth/memberUser/refresh with a structurally valid, unexpired refresh_token that is still refreshable according to backend rotation rules.
3. Verify that the endpoint validates the token, resolves it to an active member account whose lifecycle fields permit continued access (account_status active, not deleted, not closed, not fully restricted).
4. Assert that the response status is 200 and the body matches IDiscussionBoardMemberuser.IAuthorized shape: includes member id, email, display_name, lifecycle fields, and a token block of type IAuthorizationToken.
5. Check that the returned token.access and token.refresh are new values (different from the previous tokens) and that expired_at and refreshable_until are in the future and logically consistent (refreshable_until not earlier than expired_at).
6. Optionally verify that last_login_at or activity timestamps are updated according to business rules, without altering immutable fields like created_at.
7. Confirm that subsequent authenticated calls using the new access token succeed while calls using the old access token eventually fail once it expires.

dependencies.purpose: Create and authenticate a new member user to obtain an initial refresh_token for use in the refresh test, following the new user context rule via join.

scenario.draft:
Test that token refresh fails when the provided refresh token is expired or no longer refreshable.

Workflow:
1. Establish a member user account and obtain an initial pair of tokens (access + refresh) via a prior join flow.
2. Simulate passage of time or explicitly construct a scenario where the stored refresh token is past its refreshable_until boundary or otherwise marked as expired/invalid by the backend.
3. Call POST /auth/memberUser/refresh with this expired/invalid refresh_token in the IDiscussionBoardMemberUserRefresh.IRequest payload.
4. Verify that the server rejects the request with an appropriate 4xx status (e.g., 401/403) and does not issue new tokens.
5. Confirm that no changes are made to the user’s lifecycle attributes and that any error payload clearly indicates a token-expiration or invalid-token condition from a client perspective.
6. Optionally confirm that retrying with the same expired token produces the same failure and that using a still-valid token from a different session succeeds, reinforcing correct token scoping and revocation behavior.

dependencies.purpose: Register a member user and obtain a valid token pair as the historical basis for an eventually expired refresh token scenario.

scenario.draft:
Test that refresh is rejected when the member user account has transitioned into a restricted or blocked lifecycle state after token issuance.

Workflow:
1. Create a new member user via join and obtain valid access and refresh tokens.
2. Through administrative processes outside this test (or via database seeding), transition the user’s account_status and/or associated restriction record to a state that business rules consider blocked (e.g., banned, suspended, or permanently restricted).
3. Without logging in again, attempt to refresh tokens by calling POST /auth/memberUser/refresh with the previously issued refresh_token.
4. Ensure the backend checks current account status and restriction data and rejects the refresh attempt with a suitable 4xx status code.
5. Assert that no new tokens are returned (the token block is absent) and the response communicates that the account is not allowed to refresh.
6. Confirm that the underlying member profile is unchanged except for any audit-related timestamps or logs, and that subsequent refresh attempts continue to fail as long as the restriction remains in place.

dependencies.purpose: Provision a fresh member account and initial token set prior to simulating a blocked or restricted state for refresh testing.

scenario.draft:
Test server behavior when the refresh request payload is structurally invalid while still focusing on business-level handling rather than schema enforcement.

Workflow:
1. Register a member user via join and obtain a valid refresh token for baseline comparison.
2. Prepare a refresh request where the refresh_token field is present but contains an obviously malformed or tampered token string (for example, wrong signature, corrupted segments, or an incorrect token type) while still matching the IDiscussionBoardMemberUserRefresh.IRequest schema type (string).
3. Call POST /auth/memberUser/refresh with this malformed refresh_token.
4. Verify that the server correctly treats this as an invalid token rather than a validation error, returning an appropriate 4xx response and no new tokens.
5. Confirm that the member account’s lifecycle fields are not changed and that subsequent refresh attempts with a genuine, uncorrupted token still succeed, demonstrating that malformed token attempts do not poison otherwise valid sessions.

dependencies.purpose: Create a legitimate member account and obtain a reference valid refresh token to contrast with malformed token behavior in the refresh endpoint.

scenario.draft:
Test successful administrator registration and initial token issuance.

Workflow:
1. Call POST /auth/adminUser/join with a well-formed IDiscussionBoardAdminUserJoin.IRequest payload including a unique email, strong password, display_name, optional bio, and realistic href/referrer URIs.
2. Verify that the API responds with 201/200 and a body conforming to IDiscussionBoardAdminuser.IAuthorized, including id, loginId, displayName, email, status, role, emailVerified, createdAt, updatedAt, and token (IAuthorizationToken).
3. Confirm that the email returned matches the requested email, that loginId/displayName reflect the supplied values or expected transformations, and that emailVerified and status are initialized according to business defaults (e.g., emailVerified false, status active).
4. Assert that token.access and token.refresh are non-empty, syntactically valid JWTs and that expired_at and refreshable_until are future timestamps with a sensible interval.
5. Optionally perform a follow-up authenticated request to an adminUser-protected API using the returned access token to validate that the new admin account is immediately usable.

Test that administrator registration fails when using an email address that already exists in discussion_board_adminusers.

Workflow:
1. First, register an admin account via POST /auth/adminUser/join with a specific email and valid credential/profile data.
2. Attempt a second registration request to POST /auth/adminUser/join using the same email but otherwise valid IDiscussionBoardAdminUserJoin.IRequest payload (password, display_name, href, referrer, etc.).
3. Verify that the second call fails with an appropriate 4xx status (e.g., 409 conflict), indicating that the email uniqueness constraint has been enforced.
4. Ensure that no additional admin user row is created and that the original account remains unchanged.
5. Optionally validate that altering the email to a new unique value with the same other fields results in a successful registration, confirming that the failure is specifically tied to email duplication.

Test that admin join behaves correctly when only required fields are supplied and optional bio is omitted, while still creating a fully functional account.

Workflow:
1. Construct an IDiscussionBoardAdminUserJoin.IRequest payload providing email, password, display_name, href, and referrer, leaving bio explicitly null or omitting it as per schema rules.
2. Call POST /auth/adminUser/join and validate a successful response with IDiscussionBoardAdminuser.IAuthorized.
3. Confirm that the resulting admin profile has bio set to null (or equivalent) and that no other unexpected defaults are missing.
4. Verify that emailVerified and status are correctly initialized and that createdAt and updatedAt are populated.
5. Optionally, perform a quick login (if a separate login endpoint exists) to ensure that the account created with minimal required fields is fully operational.

Test that connection metadata fields (ip, href, referrer) are accepted and can be used for session/audit behavior when joining as an admin user.

Workflow:
1. Prepare an IDiscussionBoardAdminUserJoin.IRequest payload with realistic values for href and referrer URIs and a plausible ip string (or null, depending on client behavior), in addition to valid email, password, display_name, and optional bio.
2. Invoke POST /auth/adminUser/join and assert a successful response with IDiscussionBoardAdminuser.IAuthorized.
3. Verify that the join operation itself succeeds regardless of ip presence, as long as href and referrer meet URI format requirements.
4. Optionally, depending on the broader system, verify via a follow-up adminUser session inspection endpoint (if available) that the connection metadata (ip, href, referrer) has been captured in the relevant admin session records, confirming that this endpoint integrates correctly with session tracking and auditing features.

Validate that a discussion-board article category created by an admin can be retrieved publicly by its business code.

Workflow:
1. Call POST /auth/adminUser/join to create a fresh adminUser context and obtain admin authentication tokens.
2. With the admin authorization, call POST /discussionBoard/adminUser/articleCategories using IDiscussionBoardArticleCategory.ICreate to create a new category (e.g., code="ECONOMY", name="Economy", description set or null, and a valid non-negative order).
3. Capture the created category's code from the response; this is the `categoryCode` path parameter.
4. Without sending any Authorization header (since the GET is public), call GET /discussionBoard/articleCategories/{categoryCode} using the code from step 3.
5. Assert 200 OK and that the response body is a valid IDiscussionBoardArticleCategory with matching code, name, description, order, and non-null created_at/updated_at, and deleted_at is null.

- Only authenticated member users can manage their own preferences.
- A realistic onboarding flow: registration → initial content creation → notification settings configuration.
- Server correctly persists and echoes back all three preference flags for the associated member record.

scenario.draft:
Ensure that repeated PUT requests with the same payload for a member user are idempotent, not creating duplicate rows and keeping preference state stable.

Workflow:
1. Register a member via POST /auth/memberUser/join and obtain its token.
2. Register an admin via POST /auth/adminUser/join and create one category with POST /discussionBoard/adminUser/articleCategories.
3. With the member token, create one article via POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/articles using the created category.
4. Construct a IDiscussionBoardMemberuserNotificationPreference.IUpdate payload (e.g., activity_notifications_enabled=true, digest_notifications_enabled=false, marketing_notifications_enabled=true).
5. Call PUT /discussionBoard/memberUser/notifications/memberUser/preferences with this payload and store the returned IDiscussionBoardMemberuserNotificationPreference object (id, created_at, updated_at, and flags).
6. Call the same PUT again with identical payload and compare responses: the `id` and `created_at` should remain the same, and the three flag values must still match the payload. `updated_at` may be refreshed depending on implementation, but there must not be a second preference record.
7. If there is a separate GET /discussionBoard/memberUser/notifications/memberUser/preferences endpoint available, use it to confirm that only a single preference record exists for the member and that the stored flags match the latest PUT.

Business rules validated:
- Preference storage is 1:1 per member and PUT behaves idempotently.
- No duplicate notification preference records are created by repeated identical updates.
- The system consistently applies and preserves the specified flag values across multiple identical requests.

scenario.draft:
Test that an authenticated member user can successfully create a new discussion article when providing a valid existing category and valid content fields.

Workflow:
1. Call POST /auth/memberUser/join to create a fresh member user context and obtain JWT access token.
2. As an authenticated admin, create a new article category via POST /discussionBoard/adminUser/articleCategories with a unique code, name, and order so it can be referenced by articles.
3. Using the member user token from step 1, call POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/articles with a request body matching IDiscussionBoardArticle.ICreate, including a non-empty title, body, optional summary, and the categoryId returned from step 2.
4. Assert that the response status indicates success, and the response body matches IDiscussionBoardArticle: it should contain a generated UUID id, echo the title/body/summary, embed category summary matching the created category, set a valid moderationState, and populate createdAt/updatedAt.
5. Optionally verify that system-managed fields such as moderationState and timestamps are not client-controlled by confirming they are set by the server.

Business validation focus:
- Member-auth-only access to article creation.
- Foreign-key integrity with an existing category.
- Proper initialization of moderation state and audit timestamps.

scenario.draft:
Test that a member user who authored an article can successfully update that article’s content and category.

Workflow:
1. Register a new member user via POST /auth/memberUser/join and obtain the access token.
2. Register an admin user via POST /auth/adminUser/join and obtain the admin access token.
3. As the admin, create an initial article category via POST /discussionBoard/adminUser/articleCategories (Category A).
4. As the member, create an article via POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/articles using Category A and valid title/body/summary; capture the returned articleId.
5. As the admin, create a second category via POST /discussionBoard/adminUser/articleCategories (Category B) to serve as the new classification.
6. Using the same member user token, call PUT /discussionBoard/memberUser/articles/{articleId} with a body matching IDiscussionBoardArticle.IUpdate that changes the title, body, summary, and sets discussion_board_article_category_id to Category B.
7. Assert that the response is successful and that the returned IDiscussionBoardArticle reflects updated title/body/summary, the category summary now pointing to Category B, and an updated updatedAt timestamp later than the original, while id and createdAt remain unchanged.

Business validation focus:
- Only authenticated member users can update their own articles.
- Category change respects foreign-key integrity to an existing category.
- Audit timestamp updatedAt is refreshed while createdAt and id remain stable.

scenario.draft:
Validate that an authenticated adminUser can successfully create a comment on an article originally authored by a member user.

Workflow:
1. Use the adminUser join endpoint to create a fresh administrative user context and obtain JWT tokens.
2. Use the memberUser join endpoint to create a fresh member user context and obtain member JWT tokens.
3. As the member user (using the memberUser token), create an article category via the admin category creation dependency is not accessible; instead rely on the admin-created category from step 4.
4. As the admin user (using the adminUser token), create a new article category with a unique code and display order so that it can be referenced by member-created articles.
5. As the member user, call POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/articles with a valid IDiscussionBoardArticle.ICreate body referencing the admin-created category id to create an article and capture its articleId.
6. As the admin user, call POST /discussionBoard/adminUser/articles/{articleId}/comments with a valid IDiscussionBoardComment.ICreate body that contains a non-empty comment body, using the articleId from step 5, and the adminUser’s Authorization header.
7. Assert that the response status indicates success (e.g., 201/200) and that the response body is a full IDiscussionBoardComment where:
   - article.id equals the articleId used in the path.
   - author_type indicates an admin-type author.
   - body matches the submitted comment text.
   - status, created_at, and updated_at are correctly populated and deleted_at is null.
8. Optionally fetch the article’s comments list via an existing listing endpoint (already covered elsewhere) to ensure the newly created admin comment appears in the context of the article.

Business logic focus:
- Admins, once authenticated, can comment on member-authored content.
- The comment is persisted with correct article linkage and admin authorship metadata.
- Basic integrity of timestamps and moderation status is preserved.

- Comment ownership is correctly resolved: the same member who created the comment can edit it.
- Updates are limited to mutable fields while identifiers and relationships remain stable.
- Timestamps reflect modification history correctly.

scenario.draft:
Validate that a memberUser cannot update a comment authored by a different member, ensuring ownership rules are enforced.

Workflow:
1. Use the memberUser join endpoint to create Member A and obtain token A.
2. Use the memberUser join endpoint again to create Member B and obtain token B.
3. Use the adminUser join endpoint to create an admin and obtain a token, then create an article category via POST /discussionBoard/adminUser/articleCategories.
4. As Member A, create an article via POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/articles referencing the category and capture articleId.
5. As Member A, create a comment via POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/articles/{articleId}/comments and capture commentId.
6. As Member B, attempt to update that comment by calling PUT /discussionBoard/memberUser/articles/{articleId}/comments/{commentId} with an IDiscussionBoardComment.IUpdate body containing new text, using token B.
7. Assert that the response status is 403 Forbidden (or equivalent) and that no change to the comment body is persisted.
8. Optionally retrieve the comment via GET /discussionBoard/articles/{articleId}/comments/{commentId} (already covered) to confirm the body remains unchanged from Member A’s original content.

Business logic focus:
- Enforces strict per-comment ownership: only the original member author can update their comment.
- Authenticated but unrelated members cannot modify others’ comments.
- Error handling for unauthorized modification attempts is explicit and consistent.

scenario.draft:

Workflow:
1. Use the memberUser join endpoint to create a member and obtain a token.
2. Use the adminUser join endpoint to create an admin and obtain a token, then create an article category via POST /discussionBoard/adminUser/articleCategories.
3. As the member, create an article via POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/articles with the category and capture articleId.

- Comments that have been logically deleted are no longer editable, even by their original authors.
- Soft deletion semantics are respected by the update endpoint to preserve audit trails and moderation decisions.

scenario.draft:
Test that an authenticated admin user can successfully update their own profile fields (displayName, bio, and optionally accountStatus) while keeping email unique and maintaining security constraints.

Workflow:
1. Call POST /auth/adminUser/join to register a new admin with a unique email and initial profile; capture issued access token and the created adminUser id.
2. Using the access token, call POST /discussionBoard/adminUser/articleCategories to create a dummy category record; this indirectly ensures that an admin account exists in the system and exercises an admin-only write flow before profile maintenance.
3. Call PUT /discussionBoard/adminUser/adminUsers/{adminUserId} with the same adminUserId from step 1, sending an IDiscussionBoardAdminuser.IUpdate payload that updates displayName and bio (and optionally accountStatus) while leaving email unchanged.
4. Assert HTTP 200/204 success according to implementation, and verify in the response body (IDiscussionBoardAdminuser) that:
   - id matches the path adminUserId.
   - displayName and bio reflect the updated values.
   - email remains unchanged and still looks valid.
   - accountStatus is a valid business value (e.g., remains "active" if not modified).
   - createdAt remains the original creation time while updatedAt is later than createdAt.
5. Optionally re-fetch the admin user via GET /discussionBoard/adminUser/adminUsers/{adminUserId} (if used as a dependency in broader plans) to confirm persistence of updated fields.

Business rules and validations:
- Verify that only profile metadata and lifecycle flags change; sensitive fields like password are not exposed or modifiable.
- Confirm that unique email constraint is not violated by this update since the email is unchanged.
- Ensure the operation is rejected if the access token is missing or not an adminUser token (covered in separate negative scenario).

scenario.draft:
Ensure that the statistics-by-target endpoint correctly respects statusList and actionList filters when aggregating report counts.

Workflow:
1. Call POST /auth/adminUser/join to create a new adminUser and get JWT tokens.
2. Use the admin token to create an article category via POST /discussionBoard/adminUser/articleCategories.
3. As a member user, create an article via POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/articles using the category.

As a member user, create multiple reports via POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/reports targeting that article, with different combinations of status and action ultimately persisted via separate admin workflows (e.g., some staying in "submitted", others updated later to "resolved" with actions like "keep" or "delete_content" in separate tests). - Response status is 200 and body matches IDiscussionBoardReportStatisticsByTarget.
- For the target_type bucket corresponding to the reported article, totalReportCount reflects only reports whose status is in statusList and whose action is in actionList, ignoring reports with other statuses or actions.
- If there are reports for the same target_type outside the specified statusList or actionList, they are excluded from the aggregation.
- When calling again with different filter combinations (e.g., only resolved statuses or a different action list), the counts in the same bucket change accordingly, demonstrating that filters are applied before grouping.

scenario.draft:
Validate that an adminUser can retrieve aggregated report statistics grouped by reason_code and that counts per reason match underlying data.

Workflow:
1. Call POST /auth/adminUser/join to create an adminUser and obtain JWT tokens.
2. Use the admin context to create an article category via POST /discussionBoard/adminUser/articleCategories.
3. As a member user, create one or more articles via POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/articles.
4. As a member user, create multiple reports via POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/reports targeting those articles, using different category values in IDiscussionBoardReport.ICreate that map to distinct reason_code values (e.g., "spam", "hate_abuse", "off_topic").
5. As the adminUser, call PATCH /discussionBoard/adminUser/reports/statistics/byReason with a minimal IDiscussionBoardReportByReasonStatistics.IRequest (no filters) to aggregate across all reports.

Assertions:
- Response status is 200 and the body adheres to IDiscussionBoardReportByReasonStatistics.
- items array contains one row per distinct reason_code used when creating reports.
- For each reason code, total_count equals the number of created reports using that category/reason.
- The sum of total_count over all rows equals the total number of created reports.
- submitted_count, in_review_count, resolved_count, and action_*_count fields are internally consistent (e.g., submitted_count + in_review_count + resolved_count equals total_count if all statuses are mutually exclusive).

scenario.draft:

scenario.draft:

1) Call POST /auth/adminUser/join to create a new admin account and obtain JWT tokens for the adminUser actor (new user context via join only).

scenario.draft:
Validate that an admin user can retrieve the member user reporter information for a report that targets a comment.

Workflow:
1. Admin authentication: create a new admin context using /auth/adminUser/join and capture the admin JWT; this token will be used only for the final GET call.
2. Member setup and article creation: create a new member user context using /auth/memberUser/join (implicit from authorizationActor on member endpoints), obtain the member token, then call POST /discussionBoard/adminUser/articleCategories (using the admin token) to create an article category, and finally call POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/articles with the member token to create an article in that category.
3. Comment creation: using the member token and the created articleId, call POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/articles/{articleId}/comments to create a comment.
4. Report creation for comment: using the same member token, call POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/reports with a request body shaped as IDiscussionBoardReport.ICreate that sets category and reason and specifies target_comment_id equal to the created comment id while leaving target_article_id and target_attachment_id null. Capture the returned report id.
5. Reporter lookup: using the admin token, call GET /discussionBoard/adminUser/reports/{reportId}/reporter/memberUser with the reportId from step 4.

Validation points:
- The GET call succeeds only when authorized as adminUser (non-admin tokens or no auth would be rejected by guards in implementation, although those negative paths are out of scope here).
- Response type matches IDiscussionBoardReportOfMemberUser.IInvert: the discussion_board_report_id equals the created report id, discussion_board_memberuser_id matches the reporting member, and the nested report and memberUser summaries contain consistent metadata (reason_code, status, action, member display_name, account_status, etc.).
- The reporter association must exist only for member-originated reports; if the report had been created by an adminUser instead, this endpoint would reasonably return not found. This scenario ensures the positive path for a member reporter on a comment is handled.
- The link should remain valid regardless of later changes to the underlying member account status (e.g., restrictions); this scenario focuses on initial creation state but can assert that the memberUser summary reflects the current account_status at retrieval time.

scenario.draft:
Validate that an authenticated member user can successfully create a report for an article.

Scenario steps:
1) Call POST /auth/memberUser/join to create a fresh member user context and obtain JWT tokens (new user context, no login mixing).
2) As the new member user, call POST /discussionBoard/adminUser/articleCategories via an admin-created fixture (category is a prerequisite to create articles) is already covered elsewhere, so in this scenario assume a valid categoryId is provided from seeded data.
3) Using the member’s access token, call POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/articles with a valid IDiscussionBoardArticle.ICreate payload that references an existing categoryId to create a parent article; capture articleId from the response.
4) With the same member token, call POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/reports with an IDiscussionBoardReport.ICreate payload that:
   - sets category to a valid reason_code such as "spam",
   - sets reason to a non-empty explanation,
   - sets target_article_id to the created articleId, while leaving target_comment_id and target_attachment_id absent.
5) Assert that the response status indicates success (201/200) and that the returned IDiscussionBoardReport resource:
   - has target_type set to "article",
   - has reason_code equal to the requested category,
   - has non-empty id and created_at fields,
   - does not expose internal moderation-only fields beyond what the schema defines.
6) Optionally fetch the report again via an admin listing endpoint (already covered elsewhere) to verify persistence and linkage.

This test focuses on the happy-path creation of a report against an article by a normal member user, ensuring correct target inference and mandatory field handling.

scenario.draft:
Validate that an admin user can retrieve accurate aggregated report statistics by status when the system contains a realistic mix of article, comment, and attachment reports.

Workflow:
1. Call POST /auth/adminUser/join to create a new admin account and obtain admin JWT tokens; this will be used for the statistics call.
2. Call POST /auth/memberUser/join to register a new member; obtain the member’s JWT token for creating content and reports.
3. As the member, call POST /discussionBoard/adminUser/articleCategories (authorized by adminUser token) first to create a category, then POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/articles to create at least one article in that category.
4. As the member, call POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/articles/{articleId}/comments to create at least one comment on the article.
5. As the member, call POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/articles/{articleId}/attachments to register at least one attachment for the article.
6. As the member, call POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/reports multiple times to create reports covering:
   - An article-only report (target_article_id set)
   - A comment-only report (target_comment_id set)
   - An attachment-only report (target_attachment_id set)
   Use different `category` values and reasons, but ensure all are successfully created.
7. As the admin, call PATCH /discussionBoard/adminUser/reports/statistics/byStatus with a request body that does not restrict filters (only a wide time range, or even an empty filter object) so that all of the above reports are included.
8. Assert that the response returns IDiscussionBoardReportByStatusStatistics with at least one IItem for the initial status (such as "submitted") and that the total count equals the number of created reports. If multiple status buckets exist, ensure their summed count equals the total created reports included by the filters.
9. Verify that no unauthorized access occurs and that the endpoint is callable only with adminUser credentials.

Business validation:
- Confirms that analytics correctly count reports regardless of target type (article, comment, attachment).
- Ensures the grouping by status matches underlying discussion_board_reports rows.
- Verifies that combining different content activities still results in coherent status-based aggregation for moderation dashboards.

scenario.draft:
Verify that an admin can retrieve report statistics grouped by status using fine-grained filters on reason codes and time ranges, and that only matching reports are included in the aggregation.

Workflow:
1. Call POST /auth/adminUser/join to register an admin and obtain an admin token for the statistics call.
2. Call POST /auth/memberUser/join to create a member for generating content and reports.
3. As the admin, create an article category with POST /discussionBoard/adminUser/articleCategories.
4. As the member, create an article with POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/articles using the created category.
5. As the member, create at least two comments on that article with POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/articles/{articleId}/comments.
6. As the member, create multiple reports via POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/reports:
   - A report with category mapped to a reason_code such as "spam" created at time T1.
   - Another report with a different category (e.g., "off_topic") created at time T2.
   Ensure that T1 and T2 are separated enough to test created_at filters.
7. As the admin, call PATCH /discussionBoard/adminUser/reports/statistics/byStatus with IDiscussionBoardReportByStatusStatistics.IRequest specifying:
   - createdAtFrom and createdAtTo that only include the time window around T1.
   - reasonCodes including only the reason code corresponding to the first report (e.g., ["spam"]).
8. Assert that the returned statistics include counts only for reports that match the filter (the first report) and exclude the second one. Check that the status bucket counts correspond exactly to the number of filtered reports.
9. Optionally, perform a second call with a window that includes both T1 and T2 and broadened reasonCodes to verify that counts increase accordingly.

Business validation:
- Confirms that time-window and reason-code filters in IDiscussionBoardReportByStatusStatistics.IRequest are correctly applied before grouping.
- Ensures that analytics views used for moderation dashboards can be scoped to specific campaigns or time ranges.
- Validates that non-matching reports do not affect the returned status counts.

scenario.draft:
Ensure that retrieving notification preferences for a member user behaves correctly when the member is under a restriction, confirming that preferences remain readable and aligned with moderation state.

Workflow:
1. Call POST /auth/memberUser/join to create a member account and capture the memberUserId (from the authorized response) and their JWT token.
2. Call POST /auth/adminUser/join to create an admin account and obtain an admin token.
3. As the admin, optionally create categories via POST /discussionBoard/adminUser/articleCategories and have the member create an article, comments, and attachments using:
   - POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/articles
   - POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/articles/{articleId}/comments
   - POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/articles/{articleId}/attachments
   to establish some activity for this member.
4. As the admin, apply a restriction to the member via POST /discussionBoard/adminUser/memberUsers/{memberUserId}/restriction, using a restriction level such as posting_restriction and an appropriate reason_category.
5. As the restricted member, call GET /discussionBoard/memberUser/notifications/memberUser/preferences.
6. Assert that the response still successfully returns IDiscussionBoardMemberuserNotificationPreference for that member, and that no authorization error is thrown purely due to restriction state.
7. Optionally, cross-check changes in downstream behavior (in separate tests) to ensure notifications may be suppressed when restriction_level implies limited activity, but that the preferences consult view remains intact.

Business validation:
- Confirms that member restriction (discussion_board_memberuser_restrictions) does not block the user from reading their own notification preferences.
- Ensures that admin-imposed restriction state and member-configured notification preferences can coexist and be evaluated together by the notification system.
- Supports moderation requirements that even restricted users can inspect how the system intends to notify them about account and content events.

scenario.draft:
Verify that each member user can only retrieve their own notification preferences and that preferences are not shared or leaked between different members.

Workflow:
1. Call POST /auth/memberUser/join to create Member A and obtain their JWT token and memberUserId.
2. Call POST /auth/memberUser/join again to create Member B and obtain their JWT token and memberUserId.
3. Optionally, use an admin (POST /auth/adminUser/join and POST /discussionBoard/adminUser/articleCategories) to create categories and have each member create separate articles, comments, and attachments via:
   - POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/articles
   - POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/articles/{articleId}/comments
   - POST /discussionBoard/memberUser/articles/{articleId}/attachments
   so that both members have independent activity contexts.
4. As Member A, call GET /discussionBoard/memberUser/notifications/memberUser/preferences and store the returned IDiscussionBoardMemberuserNotificationPreference values.
5. As Member B, call the same GET endpoint and store B’s returned preferences.
6. Assert that each call returns a valid preference object and that identifiers (such as discussion_board_memberuser_id) in each response correspond to the authenticated member, not the other member.
7. Confirm that Member A’s token cannot retrieve Member B’s preference record (the endpoint should always use the authenticated identity from the session, ignoring any client attempt to influence user selection).

Business validation:
- Ensures that notification preferences are strictly per-member and bound to the authenticated user context.
- Prevents data leakage where one member might view or infer another member’s notification settings.
- Confirms that the API implementation correctly uses session identity rather than any user-supplied identifiers when reading preferences.
